name: Mary, mother of Jesus
info: Mary was a first-century Jewish woman of Nazareth, the wife of Joseph and the mother of Jesus, venerated in Christianity under many titles and honoured in Islam, where a chapter of the Quran bears her name.

facts.born: Date not recorded; a Jewish woman of Nazareth in Galilee, betrothed to Joseph; the Gospel of James, a later text, names her parents as Joachim and Anne
facts.died: Not recorded in the Bible; Hyppolitus of Thebes, writing in the 7th or 8th century, says she died in 41 CE; Orthodox tradition holds that she died naturally (the Dormition) and was then taken bodily into Heaven
facts.role: Mother of Jesus and wife of Joseph; held by Eastern and Oriental Orthodox, Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and Methodist churches to be the Mother of God; historians know her chiefly through the Gospels and Acts
facts.known: the annunciation by the angel Gabriel; the birth of Jesus at Bethlehem; presence at the wedding at Cana and at the crucifixion; the Magnificat; Theotokos, proclaimed at the Council of Ephesus in 431; the Assumption; the only woman named in the Quran

t: The Gospels of Matthew and Luke describe Mary as a virgin chosen by God to conceive Jesus through the Holy Spirit, and they place her at the birth of Jesus, in Nazareth, and at his crucifixion.
Little is recorded of her life: the Bible does not describe her death, and the later accounts of her parents, childhood and end are scholars' and churches' traditions rather than firm history.
Churches differ widely over her: Catholics and the Orthodox hold distinctive beliefs and devotions, most Protestants honour her without venerating her, and the Quran gives her a chapter of her own.
dyk: Mary is the only woman named in the Quran, which mentions or refers to her 50 times and gives one chapter her name, while the earliest known prayer to her, the Sub tuum praesidium, was found on a papyrus in Egypt in 1917.
ev: Mary, betrothed to Joseph, is told by the angel Gabriel that she will conceive Jesus through the Holy Spirit, as Luke tells it
She gives birth to Jesus in Bethlehem, according to Luke during a Roman census, and presents him at the Temple in Jerusalem
At her suggestion Jesus works his first miracle at the wedding at Cana, in the Gospel of John
She stands near the cross at the crucifixion of Jesus, in John's account
Acts names her with the apostles and the brothers of Jesus in the upper room after the Ascension
The Council of Ephesus declares her Theotokos, the God-bearer
Pope Pius IX proclaims the Immaculate Conception
Pope Pius XII defines the Assumption in Munificentissimus Deus

sections.early:
The New Testament tells little of Mary's early history. Her name comes from the Hebrew Miryam, rendered Mariam or Maria in Greek. The earliest mention is in the letter to the Galatians, written before the Gospels, which speaks of God's Son as born of a woman without naming her. The Gospel of Luke calls her a relative of Elizabeth, the wife of the priest Zechariah, and Matthew gives a genealogy only for Joseph, her husband. The Gospel of James, a later text that scholars generally treat as historically unreliable, gives her parents as Joachim and Anne and says she was given to service in the Temple at three years old. Some of those who think her relationship with Elizabeth was on her mother's side hold that Mary too was of the royal line of David, though Matthew and Luke give no such genealogy for her.

The Gospels place her at Nazareth in Galilee, betrothed to Joseph, the first stage of a Jewish marriage. Jewish girls were considered marriageable at twelve and a half, though the actual age varied. Scholars hold that Jewish girls typically married between the mid teens and early twenties, and the Gospels do not give her age. The Gospels were composed from about 66 to 110 CE, and historians note that early Christian writings often mixed historical fact with legend.
sections.rise:
In the Gospel of Luke the angel Gabriel tells Mary that she is to conceive the promised Messiah through the Holy Spirit. After some questioning she answers, in Luke's words, "I am the handmaid of the Lord. Let it be done unto me according to your word." Matthew adds that Joseph planned to divorce her quietly until an angel told him in a dream that the child was conceived by the Holy Spirit, and he took her as his wife. Christians hold that she remained a virgin while conceiving Jesus, a belief that was almost universal among Christians from the 2nd to the 19th century.

Luke tells that Mary hurried to Elizabeth, who greeted her as the mother of her Lord. Mary then spoke the words of praise that became known as the Magnificat, and she returned home after about three months. A decree of Augustus brought her and Joseph to Bethlehem, where she gave birth to Jesus and used a manger as a cradle. Jesus was circumcised after eight days, and after 40 days she brought her offering to the Temple in Jerusalem. According to Matthew the family fled to Egypt from Herod and settled again in Nazareth after Herod's death in 4 BCE.
sections.deeds:
Mary appears in few scenes of the ministry. When Jesus was twelve, Luke tells, he stayed behind in the Temple at Passover and she found him among the teachers. The Gospel of John places her at the wedding at Cana, where at her suggestion Jesus performs his first miracle by turning water into wine. John calls him addressing her as Woman, which in Koine Greek was not disrespectful and could be tender. It is the only passage in which the adult Jesus speaks with her.

She is mentioned along with his brothers, whose identity is disputed. Epiphanius, Origen and Eusebius held that they were sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage, which remains the position of the Eastern Orthodox Church. Jerome held that they were cousins, the Roman Catholic position, while Helvidius held that they were full siblings, the commonest Protestant view. John places her at the crucifixion, near the disciple whom Jesus loved. Acts 1:14 names her as the only woman other than the apostles in the upper room after the Ascension. The Book of Revelation's woman clothed with the sun is sometimes identified as Mary.
sections.opponents:
The Gospels record no persecution of Mary herself. They do record friction within her family: Mark says that Jesus's mother and brothers came to take him because people said he was out of his mind, and Jesus answers that those who do the will of God are his mother and brothers. The Gospels also show Joseph fearing her pregnancy and Herod seeking the child.

Belief in her virginity was disputed early. In the 2nd century the pagan philosopher Celsus, in The True Word, contended that Jesus was the illegitimate son of a Roman soldier named Panthera, and Origen dismissed this as a complete fabrication in Against Celsus. The Toledot Yeshu, a medieval Jewish text that circulated widely in Europe and the Middle East from the 9th century, told the story of Panthera and gave Jewish readers a negative picture of Mary; scholars such as Raymond E. Brown and Robert Van Voorst consider it a late and fanciful source with little historical value. After a disputation in 1240 copies of the Talmud were burnt on a court order for allegedly defaming her.

Biblical scholars still debate what Matthew 1:25 means by "until", and whether the Hebrew almah, a young woman, was rightly rendered by the Greek parthenos in Isaiah 7:14. Bart Ehrman is among those who note the difference. Matthew and Luke give differing versions of the birth.
sections.last:
Her death is not recorded in the Bible. Acts leaves her with the apostles after the Ascension, and Christian tradition holds that she was present at Pentecost, though the text does not say so. John says that Jesus asked the disciple whom he loved to look after her, and Irenaeus and Eusebius wrote that John later went to Ephesus, which may be the basis of the early belief that she lived there. A house at Ephesus is now venerated, a claim made in the 19th century from the visions of Anne Catherine Emmerich.

Hyppolitus of Thebes, in the 7th or 8th century, wrote that Mary lived 11 years after the death of her son and died in 41 CE. The earliest surviving biography of her, the Life of the Virgin, is attributed to Maximus the Confessor in the 7th century. The Eastern Orthodox hold that she died naturally, an event called the Dormition, and was then taken bodily into Heaven; Eastern Christians believe she was laid in a tomb near Jerusalem first. The Catholic Church defines the Assumption as dogma in the Latin and Eastern Churches alike, without defining whether she died, and it is believed also by the Oriental Orthodox and parts of the Anglican Communion.
sections.legacy:
Mary has been venerated since early Christianity. The Sub tuum praesidium, the oldest known prayer to her, dates to about 250 or 270 CE. The Council of Ephesus in 431 declared her Theotokos, the God-bearer, because Jesus is held to be one person who is both God and man. Pope Pius IX proclaimed the Immaculate Conception in 1854, which the Orthodox do not accept because their understanding of ancestral sin differs. The Catholic Church holds four Marian dogmas, the Mother of God, perpetual virginity, the Immaculate Conception and the Assumption, and it keeps more feasts and prayers to her than any other group, among them the Rosary. The Orthodox honour her above the angels in the Akathist Hymn.

Protestants generally reject the invocation of saints. Martin Luther honoured her, and John Calvin granted her the highest honour while denying that she can intercede. Anglicans differ among themselves, Methodists hold the virgin birth, and nontrinitarian groups acknowledge her as Jesus's mother without the title Mother of God.

In Islam, Maryam is the daughter of Imran, the Quran calls her chosen above the women of the world, and a chapter is named for her. Muslims believe in the virgin birth of Jesus, born through the Spirit. The Druze and the Baháʼí Faith also revere her. She is traditionally painted in blue, and the Council of Ephesus and the Roman feast days still shape the Christian year.

summary: Mary was a Jewish woman of Nazareth, the mother of Jesus, whom the Gospels of Matthew and Luke describe as a virgin. She is venerated across much of Christianity and holds the highest place among women in Islam, while her death is not recorded in the Bible.
references: Stephen Shoemaker, Ancient Traditions of the Virgin Mary's Dormition and Assumption (Oxford University Press, 2003)
Alphonsus Liguori, The Glories of Mary, Mother of God. Translated from the Italian (Dublin: John Coyne, 1833)
notes: No birth year in the article: start -5 is a placeholder near the date of Jesus's birth (c. 6 to 4 BC), not her own; editor may unset it. End 41 is only the late statement of Hyppolitus of Thebes, so endCirca true.

Event dates c. 6 and c. 5 BCE are inferred from the article's Herod death of 4 BC and are the editor's to check; the article gives no year for the annunciation or birth in her page. Jesus's page gives 6 to 4 BC.
The Cana year c. 28 CE and the 'c. 30 CE' upper-room date are inferred from Jesus's ministry dates on his own page, not stated in Mary's article.
Left out: Our Lady of the Pillar, apparitions and relics except in passing; the Qur'anic birth narrative from Imran's wife.
